L13@P0: ABSTRACT
L14@P0: This chapter provides an introduction to the mathematics associated with
L15@P0: combinatorial problems that have their origin in music and prosody, which
L16@P0: were studied by Indian mathematicians over the centuries starting from
L17@P0: around the third century BC. Large parts of this mathematics are accessible
L18@P0: without a knowledge of advanced mathematics, and there are several connections with what is learned in school or in early university education. The
L19@P0: chapter presents expositions of such connections with, for example, binary
L20@P0: arithmetic and Fibonacci numbers. In solving some of the problems, Indian
L21@P0: mathematicians worked implicitly with the idea that all positive integers can
L22@P0: be represented uniquely as sums of specific kinds of numbers such as the
L23@P0: powers of 2, Fibonacci numbers and factorial numbers. These ideas are
L24@P0: interesting, both in themselves and for the connections they make with
L25@P0: aspects of culture, and hold promise for mathematics education and the
L26@P0: popularization of mathematics.

L29@P1: REPRESENTATIONS OF NUMBERS AND THE INDIAN
L30@P1: MATHEMATICAL TRADITION OF COMBINATORIAL PROBLEMS
L31@P1: The history of Indian mathematics has been an area of exciting new discoveries in recent decades. Fresh insights into the contributions of the
L32@P1: Kerala mathematicians from the fourteenth to the seventeenth centuries
L33@P1: CE are among the better known discoveries. Mathematical work from earlier periods too have been more thoroughly studied and better understood. Plofker (2009) provides a recent overview of the history of Indian
L34@P1: mathematics. Several recent anthologies convey the excitement of current
L35@P1: work in the field (see e.g., Emch, Srinivas, & Sridharan, 2005; Seshadri,
L36@P1: 2010).
L37@P1: Our purpose in this chapter is to explore aspects of the history of
L38@P1: Indian mathematics that may be of interest to the mathematics education
L39@P1: community. Specifically we explore the work on combinatorial problems
L40@P1: beginning from around the third century BC and continuing till the fourteenth century CE. The problems and the mathematical ideas developed
L41@P1: by this tradition need only a level of mathematical knowledge available to
L42@P1: many secondary school students. The ideas have interesting connections
L43@P1: with Indian cultural forms, both living and historical and hence may
L44@P1: appeal to a wider audience than those with a taste for mathematics. The
L45@P1: material in this chapter is largely expository and draws heavily on the
L46@P1: recent historical work and textual interpretations of among others, R.
L47@P1: Sridharan, of whom the first author of this chapter is a collaborator (Sridharan, 2005, 2006; Sridharan, Sridharan, & Srinivas, 2010).
L48@P1: The development of numeral notation and forms in India provides a
L49@P1: backdrop for the discussion of the connections of combinatorial ideas
L50@P1: with number representations in this chapter. It is fairly well known that
L51@P1: the decimal numeral system currently used had its origins in India and
L52@P1: was transmitted to the West through contact with Arab culture. A decimal
L53@P1: system of number names with Sanskrit names for the numbers from 1 to
L54@P1: 9, and for powers of 10 up to a trillion was already developed in the second millennium BC and appears in the vedas, the oldest extant literature
L55@P1: from India (Plofker, 2009). Large numbers were denoted by compounding names for 1 to 9 with names for powers of 10, much like in present
L56@P1: day English. Besides these, once also finds in the vedic literature “concrete” number names, which are salient cardinalities (e.g., “moon” = 1,
L57@P1: “eyes” = 2, “sages” = 7 from the well known saptar i* or seven ancient
L58@P1: sages). The earliest inscriptions in which a positional decimal numeral system is used, date to the second half of the first millennium CE. However

L62@P2: much earlier evidence for positional value exists in the form textual references. For example, the year in which a work was authored is mentioned
L63@P2: as “Vi u hook-sign moon.” These are concrete number names where
L64@P2: “Vi u” (a leading diety) stands for one, “hook-sign” for nine (from the
L65@P2: shape of the written numeral) and “moon” for one. Thus the number
L66@P2: translates to “191” using decimal positional notation, a year measured in
L67@P2: the aka era, which corresponds to the year 269 or 270 CE (Plofker,
L68@P2: 2009). The order is actually right to left, which does not matter here since
L69@P2: “191” is a palindrome.
L70@P2: It must be noted that there were other numeral systems in use through
L71@P2: the centuries. Some of these were not based on positional value, like the
L72@P2: alphanumeric system used by ryabha a, the author of the foundational
L73@P2: astronomical-mathematical work ryabha !ya written in 499 CE. In this
L74@P2: system, consonants of the Sanskrit alphabet had specific numerical values
L75@P2: depending on their position in the alphabet, while vowels indicated powers of 10 (Plofker, 2009). For example, the consonant “kh” had a value of
L76@P2: 2, while the vowels “i” and “u” had respectively values of 102 and 104.
L77@P2: Thus the syllable “khi” would mean 200, while “khu” would mean 20000.
L78@P2: The syllable “ni” would denote 2000: “n” = 20 and “i” = 102. It was possible to denote the large numbers that are needed for astronomical calculations in a compact manner using ryabha a’s notation, but the syllablewords that were produced were difficult to pronounce.
L79@P2: A more popular number system was the positional value based ka apay di system in which consonants took numerical values from 0 to 9,
L80@P2: depending on their order in the Sanskrit alphabet. The first ten consonants in the first two rows of consonants in the Sanskrit alphabet (“k” to
L81@P2: “ñ”) denote, in order, the digits “1” to “0”. The next two rows also denote
L82@P2: the same digits. So this system had redundancies—three or four consonants denoted the same digit, and vowels did not have numerical value.
L83@P2: The redundancies allowed flexibility in the choice of a syllable combination to denote a number—often an actual Sanskrit word could be used to
L84@P2: denote a number. Thus the word “dh!ra” (meaning resolute or courageous) would denote 29, since “dh” denotes the digit “9” and “r” denotes
L85@P2: “2”. (Note that the order is right to left.) Of all these systems, the positional value based concrete number system described above was the most
L86@P2: widely used in mathematical texts. For more details about the various
L87@P2: number systems, see Plofker (2009).

L100@P3: existed in Indian mathematics for over two millennia. These problems
L101@P3: have their origin not in a branch of science or technology, but in the
L102@P3: arts—in prosody and in music. However, the mathematical ideas were
L103@P3: pursued for their own sake as a distinct “mathematical” tradition, beyond
L104@P3: the practical needs in poetry or music. While Sanskrit poetry largely
L105@P3: belongs to the past or is pursued by specialized groups, Indian classical
L106@P3: music is a living and vibrant aspect of contemporary Indian culture. (It
L107@P3: must be noted that prosody in modern Indian languages is heavily influenced by Sanskrit prosody.) A penchant for classification and systematic
L108@P3: organization is reflected in the classical musical traditions of India. These
L109@P3: typically take the form of specifying an underlying basic structure or
L110@P3: alphabet and enumerating melodic or rhythmic possibilities emerging
L111@P3: from the basic structure. We will first look at this aspect of classical music,
L112@P3: both with regard to melody and rhythm and then provide a brief introduction to these aspects in Sanskrit prosody. This introduction to cultural
L113@P3: aspects provides a background for better appreciation of the mathematical discussion that follows. However, the mathematical sections can be
L114@P3: understood independent of this background.
L115@P3: Combinatorics in Karn ak music. The two great streams of classical
L116@P3: music in contemporary India are Karn ak and Hindust ni music. They
L117@P3: share many characteristics and similarities, although the musical compositions, musicians and serious audiences are largely separate groups. We
L118@P3: give a brief introduction to the Karn ak musical tradition, whose geographical center is in South India, to highlight the role of combinatorial
L119@P3: structure in its melodic and rhythmic forms.
L120@P3: The melodic forms that provide the basis for both Karn ak and Hindust ni music are called r gas, which are roughly analogous to scales in
L121@P3: Western music. The basic specification of a r ga is in terms of the ascending and descending sequence of notes (svaras) in the scale. The notes are
L122@P3: expressed using the seven “solfege” syllables of Indian classical music,
L123@P3: which are pronounced as “Sa, Re, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni”, and commonly
L124@P3: notated in writing using the first letter. These are short forms for the
L125@P3: names of the notes: a ja, Ri aba, G ndh ra, Madhyama, Pancama, Dhaivata and Ni ada. The tonic Sa (or a ja) is fixed arbitrarily, and the
L126@P3: remaining notes have a specific tonal relation to the tonic. The notes have
L127@P3: higher and lower tonal values, which are shown in Table 79.1. However,
L128@P3: the seven notes correspond only to 12 distinct tone positions because of
L129@P3: overlaps. There are four pairs of duplicate names for the same position:
L130@P3: R2=G1, R3=G2, D2=N1, D3=N2. It must be noted however that in Karn ak music as it is actually performed, the tonal values of the svaras are
L131@P3: flexible (Krishnaswamy, 2003).

L97: 
L98:     गीती शीघ्री शिरःकम्पी तथा लिखितपाठकः ।
L99:     अनर्थज्ञोऽल्पकण्ठश्च षडेते पाठकाधमाः ॥ ३२॥
L100: 
L101:     माधुर्यमक्षरव्यक्तिः पदच्छेदस्तु सुस्वरः ।
L102:     धैर्यं लयसमर्थं च षडेते पाठका गुणाः ॥ ३३॥
L103:     शङ्कितं भीतिमुद्घृष्टमव्यक्तमनुनासिकम् ।
L104:     काकस्वरं शिरसिगं तथा स्थानविवजिर्तम् ॥ ३४॥
L105: 
L106:     उपांशुदष्टं त्वरितं निरस्तं विलम्बितं गद्गदितं प्रगीतम् ।
L107:     निष्पीडितं ग्रस्तपदाक्षरं च वदेन्न दीनं न तु सानुनास्यम् ॥ ३५॥
L108: 
L109:     प्रातः पठेन्नित्यमुरःस्थितेन स्वरेण शार्दूलरुतोपमेन ।
L110:     मध्यन्दिने कण्ठगतेन चैव चक्राह्वसङ्कूजितसन्निभेन ॥ ३६॥
L111: 
L112:     तारं तु विद्यात्सवनं तृतीयं शिरोगतं तच्च सदा प्रयोज्यम् ।
L113:     मयूरहंसान्यभृतस्वराणां तुल्येन नादेन शिरःस्थितेन ॥ ३७॥
L114:     अचोऽस्पृष्टा यणस्त्वीषन्नेमस्पृष्टाः शलः स्मृताः ।
L115:     शेषाः स्पृष्टा हलः प्रोक्ता निबोधानुप्रदानतः ॥ ३८॥
L116: 
L117:     ञमोनुनासिका न ह्रौ नादिनो हझषः स्मृताः ।
L118:     ईषन्नादा यणो जशः श्वासिनस्तु खफादयः ॥ ३९॥
L119: 
L120:     ईषच्छ्वासांश्चरो विद्याद्गोर्धामैतत्प्रचक्षते ।
L121:     दाक्षीपुत्रपाणिनिना येनेदं व्यापितं भुवि ॥ ४०॥
L122: 
L123:     छन्दः पादौ तु वेदस्य हस्तौ कल्पोऽथ पठ्यते ।
L124:     ज्योतिषामयनं चक्षुर्निरुक्तं श्रोत्रमुच्यते ॥ ४१॥
L125: 
L126:     शिक्षा घ्राणं तु वेदस्य मुखं व्याकरणं स्मृतम् ।
L127:     तस्मात्साङ्गमधीत्यैव ब्रह्मलोके महीयते ॥ ४२॥
L128: 
L129:     उदात्तमाख्याति वृषोऽङ्गुलीनां प्रदेशिनीमूलनिविष्टमूर्धा ।
L130:     उपान्तमध्ये स्वरितं द्रुतं च कनिष्ठकायामनुदात्तमेव ॥ ४३॥
L131: 
L132:     उदात्तं प्रदेशिनीं विद्यात्प्रचयं मध्यतोऽङ्गुलिम् ।
L133:     निहतं तु कनिष्ठिक्यां स्वरितोपकनिष्ठिकाम् ॥ ४४॥
L134: 
L135:     अन्तोदात्तमाद्युदात्तमुदात्तमनुदात्तं नीचस्वरितम् ।
L136:     मध्योदात्तं स्वरितं द्व्युदात्तं त्र्युदात्तमिति नवपदशय्या ॥ ४५॥
L137: 
L138:     अग्निः सोमः प्र वो वीर्यं हविषां स्वर्बृहस्पतिरिन्द्राबृहस्पती ।
L139:     अग्निरित्यन्तोदात्तं सोम इत्याद्युदात्तम् ।
L140:     प्रेत्युदात्तं व इत्यनुदात्तं वीर्यं नीचस्वरितम् ॥ ४६॥
L141: 
L142:     हविषां मध्योदात्तं स्वरिति स्वरितम् ।
L143:     बृहस्पतिरिति द्व्युदात्तमिन्द्राबृहस्पती इति त्र्युदात्तम् ॥ ४७॥
L144: 
L145:     अनुदात्तो हृदि ज्ञेयो मूर्ध्न्युदात्त उदाहृतः ।
L146:     स्वरितः कर्णमूलीयः सर्वास्ये प्रचयः स्मृतः ॥ ४८॥
L147: 
L148:     चाषस्तु वदते मात्रां द्विमात्रं चैव वायसः ।
L149:     शिखी रौति त्रिमात्रं तु नकुलस्त्वर्धमात्रकम् ॥ ४९॥
L150: 
L151:     कुतीर्थादागतं दग्धमपवर्णं च भक्षितम् ।
L152:     न तस्य पाठे मोक्षोऽस्ति पापाहेरिव किल्बिषात् ॥ ५०॥
L153: 
L154:     सुतीर्थादगतं व्यक्तं स्वाम्नाय्यं सुव्यवस्थितम् ।
L155:     सुस्वरेण सुवक्त्रेण प्रयुक्तं ब्रह्म राजते ॥ ५१॥
L156: 
L157:     मन्त्रो हीनः स्वरतो वर्णतो वा मिथ्याप्रयुक्तो न तमर्थमाह ।
L158:     स वाग्वज्रो यजमानं हिनस्ति यथेन्द्रशत्रुः स्वरतोऽपराधात् ॥
L159: 
L160:     अनक्षरं हतायुष्यं विस्वरं व्याधिपीडितम् ।
L161:     अक्षता शस्त्ररूपेण वज्रं पतति मस्तके ॥ ५३॥
L162: 
L163:     हस्तहीनं तु योऽधीते स्वरवर्णविवर्जितम् ।
L164:     ऋग्यजुःसामभिर्दग्धो वियोनिमधिगच्छति ॥ ५४॥
L165:     हस्तेन वेदं योऽधीते स्वरवर्णर्थसंयुतम् ।
L166:     ऋग्यजुःसामभिः पूतो ब्रह्मलोके महीयते ॥ ५५॥
L167: 
L168:     शङ्करः शाङ्करीं प्रादाद्दाक्षीपुत्राय धीमते ।
L169:     वाङ्मयेभ्यः समाहृत्य देवीं वाचमिति स्थितिः ॥ ५६॥
L170: 
L171:     येनाक्षरसमाम्नायमधिगम्य महेश्वरात् ।
L172:     कृत्स्नं व्याकरणं प्रोक्तं तस्मै पाणिनये नमः ॥ ५७॥
L173: 
L174:     येन धौता गिरः पुंसां विमलैः शब्दवारिभिः ।
L175:     तमश्चाज्ञानजं भिन्नं तस्मै पाणिनये नमः ॥ ५८॥
L176: 
L177:     अज्ञानान्धस्य लोकस्य ज्ञानाञ्जनशलाकया ।
L178:     चक्षुरुन्मीलितं येन तस्मै पाणिनये नमः ॥ ५९॥
L179:     त्रिनयनमभिमुखनिःसृतामिमां य इह पठेत्प्रयतश्च सदा द्विजः ।
L180:     स भवति धनधान्यपशुपुत्रकीर्तिमान् अतुलं च सुखं समश्नुते दिवीति दिवीति ॥ ६०॥
L181: 
L182:     ॥ इति वेदाङ्गनासिका अथवा पाणिनीयशिक्षा समाप्ता ॥
